title: Following a lecture or talk
subtitle: Main points, connections and explanations
summary: Separate a talk's main points from its asides, use a summary to keep your place, and predict the technical terms a lecturer will explain.

lesson.heading: Not everything said is a main point
lesson.text: At the start of a talk you are told who the speaker is and why they are talking. You are not tested on that, but it tells you the **purpose** of the talk - and the questions only ever ask about points that serve that purpose. Everything else is background.

examples.text: **I had to do a compulsory unit on extinction**
examples.note: main point - this is how he first became interested in palaeontology
main point - this is when he began to study it

examples.text: **I found a funny-looking piece of rock**
examples.note: main point - this encouraged him to continue

examples.text: *an old professor studying dried-up dinosaur bones*
examples.note: background - just how people picture palaeontologists

examples.text: *It's an ancestor of the modern Australian wombat*
examples.note: background - an explanation of what a Diprotodon is

examples.text: *the very first field trip I went on*
examples.note: background - nothing happened on that trip

lesson.note: Ask yourself: does this move the story forward, or just decorate it?

lesson.heading: Turn every gap into a question
lesson.text: A summary-completion task looks hard until you convert each gap into a question. Then you are listening for an answer rather than scanning for a word.

examples.text: *Paul was interested in the ___ so took an ecology course.*
examples.note: Why did Paul take an ecology course? Answer: **environment**
What did the course include? Answer: **extinction**
What are the conditions usually like? Answer: **extreme**

examples.text: *the discovery of a ___ from an ancient animal*

lesson.heading: The script and the summary say the same thing

left.label: What you hear
examples: *As a part of my degree course, I had to do a compulsory unit on ...*

right.label: What the summary says
examples: The course included a section on ...

lesson.note: The information appears in the **same order** in the summary as in the recording. That is what makes a summary useful for keeping your place.

lesson.heading: What kind of information is this?
rows: the methods used in a study
we looked at, we measured, the sample was, we compared
led to, resulted in, meant that, as a consequence
the reason an action was carried out
because, in order to, the aim was, we wanted to find out
this suggests, we can therefore say, it seems clear that
we found, the results showed, what emerged was

lesson.heading: Technical terms get explained
lesson.text: Do not panic at an unfamiliar word in the questions. In an academic talk, a technical term is nearly always defined or paraphrased the moment it appears - and the explanation is often the answer.

examples.note: The finding: a lack of exercise made the cells appear older - not that diet had no effect.

examples.text: A talk on pigeons: how they navigate.
examples.note: The new discovery is about the **ears**, not the beak or the magnetic field - those were already known.

lesson.note: An option can be wrong because it is *old news* rather than untrue. Listen for *we've known for decades* and *has been proven to be false*.

lesson.text: Write the question words next to each gap during your reading time - *what? when? why? how many?*. It takes fifteen seconds and it stops you writing a noun where the gap needs a number.

exercises.prompt: Paul explains how he became a palaeontologist. Which details serve that purpose?

items.text: I had to do a compulsory unit on extinction
I found a funny-looking piece of rock
an old professor studying dried-up dinosaur bones
It's an ancestor of the modern Australian wombat
the very first field trip I went on

exercises.prompt: *Paul was interested in the ___ so took an ecology course.* (ONE WORD ONLY)
exercises.explanation: Turning the gap into a question - *What was Paul interested in?* - is what makes it findable.

exercises.prompt: Match each extract with the type of information it gives.

pairs.left: We compared two samples over six months.
pairs.right: the methods used in a study

pairs.left: This led to a sharp fall in numbers.
The aim was to find out why they migrate.
pairs.right: the reason an action was carried out

pairs.left: We can therefore say the theory holds.
The results showed no change at all.

exercises.statement: The gaps in a summary-completion task follow the order of the recording.
exercises.explanation: That is exactly why a summary is useful: it tells you where you are in the talk, even if you miss a gap.

exercises.prompt: The question is *What new discovery have scientists made about pigeons?* You hear that pigeons use the Earth's magnetic field and that this has been known for decades. Why is that option wrong?
options: Because it uses more than two words
exercises.explanation: The question asks what is *new*. Something known for decades is a distractor even though it is perfectly true.

exercises.prompt: *He describes the conditions in the field as ___.* (ONE WORD ONLY)
exercises.explanation: *What are the conditions usually like?* - that is the question the gap is really asking.

exercises.prompt: Why are you told who the speaker is at the start of a talk?
options: Because there is a question about it
Because it gives you the purpose of the talk, which the questions follow
Because you must write the speaker's name on the answer sheet
Because the speaker changes halfway through
exercises.explanation: You are not tested on it, but it frames everything else - the questions only ask about points serving that purpose.

exercises.prompt: Build the question hidden in the gap *Paul says working in palaeontology can be ___.*
exercises.answer: What is the work usually like?
exercises.explanation: A gap after *can be* needs an adjective, so the question starts *What ... like?*

exercises.statement: If you see a technical term you do not know in the questions, you should assume that question is lost.
exercises.explanation: Technical terms are nearly always explained in the talk itself. The explanation is often exactly what the question is testing.

exercises.prompt: In a study of mice, cells either deteriorated or showed less change, and nothing was said about diet. Which option is a distractor?
options: A lack of exercise made them appear older
Their cells remained the same as they aged
exercises.explanation: The cells did change in both groups, so *remained the same* is contradicted by the recording.
